movement.name: Armenian Apostolic Church — Etchmiadzin and Constantinople
movement.informalName: The Church of the Mother See and the Capital
movement.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
movement.sourcing: Thin to moderate. The texts at hand are one catholicos's own story of 1736, a deacon's chronicle up to the 1690s, and Jesuit and Catholic Armenian writings of the time. Later histories come from both sides. No records of the see at Etchmiadzin or of the patriarchate in the capital are yet in hand.
movement.floorNote: No question — this is one of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches. It differs from the churches of Chalcedon on how to speak of Christ as God and man, not on whether he is God.
movement.relationsSummary: The head of the church, the catholicos, sat at Etchmiadzin under Persian rule. A patriarch in the sultan's capital led the Armenians of the Ottoman lands. By the sultan's law, even those who joined Rome had to obey him. Catholic missions won over a party of Armenians, and the patriarch fought back hard. The Catholic party used the French ambassadors against him in turn. In 1742 the pope approved a patriarch of their own for the Armenian Catholics. Late in the century, Armenian leaders began to look to Russia.
movement.why: For a century and a half, the main Armenian church was led from two places. Its supreme head, the catholicos, lived at Etchmiadzin, and the Persian court had to approve each election. In the Ottoman capital a patriarch led a strong Armenian community, and that city became the center of the nation. This church kept most Armenians in its fold while Rome's missions worked to win them. It also renewed itself, with new schools, a printing press and a turn toward Russia.
movement.longDescription: Two seats led the Armenian Apostolic Church in these years. The catholicos lived at Etchmiadzin, in lands ruled from Persia. The Persian court had to approve his election. A patriarch led the Armenians of Constantinople, and that city became the center of the nation. Catholic missionaries worked hard to win Armenians to Rome. One of their party once seized the patriarch's seat, but the people drove him out. At the same time a rival bishop had himself proclaimed supreme patriarch of the sultan's lands, against Etchmiadzin. In 1664 the catholicos Hacob IV went to Constantinople to restore order. He died there on a second journey in 1680. The quarrel grew bitter. The patriarch's side had the Ottoman government act against Armenians who had become Catholics. The Catholic side, for its part, used the French ambassadors against the patriarch. In 1703 the patriarch Avedik was put in prison when the French ambassador stepped in. Later he was carried off to France, where he died. Catholic writers record that in 1707 the patriarch John handed the priest Gomidas to the Turks, accusing him of following the Franks. "I am a Christian and a follower of St. Gregory the Illuminator, Armenian by birth," Gomidas told them. He was beheaded. In 1742 the pope approved a separate Armenian Catholic patriarchate. Even so, a Catholic Armenian wrote in 1783 that his people still had to obey the patriarch. They still went to his churches to baptize, marry and bury. In 1722 Afghan armies reached Isfahan, and the Armenians of New Julfa had to ransom their town more than once. In 1736 the catholicos Abraham of Crete went to Nadir's camp on the Mughan plain, where an assembly asked Nadir to rule Persia. Abraham was one of three men chosen to speak for the Armenians, and he came home with seven written orders he had asked for. From 1763 to 1780 the catholicos Simeon of Erevan founded a college, brought in printing and built a paper mill. He also opened the church's first ties with the Russian empire. As Persian rule grew harsher, Armenians began to look to the czar. In 1810 a new catholicos, Ephraim, came to Etchmiadzin under a guard of Russian soldiers.
movement.teaser: Etchmiadzin and Constantinople, 1650 to 1815 — the main Armenian church. It was led from a holy see under Persian rule and from the sultan's capital, and it held its people while Rome worked to win them.
voices: Hacob IV of Julfa — head of the church from 1655 to 1680, who went to the sultan's capital in 1664 to restore order
Gomidas — a priest put to death in 1707; Catholic writers say his own patriarch turned him over to the Turks
Abraham of Crete — catholicos from 1734 to 1737, who wrote his own account of Nadir Shah's rise to the throne in 1736
Simeon of Erevan — head of the church from 1763 to 1780, who set up a school, a press and the first ties with Russia
Zakaria Pokouzian — patriarch in the sultan's capital from 1773 to 1799, who taught his priests himself and put them in charge of schools
movement.legacy: Much of what this church built in these years lasted. Simeon of Erevan's new church calendar met protest at first. Within a short time, every Armenian church used it. Pupils of the patriarch Zakaria founded the college at Armash, which gave the church many later patriarchs and bishops. In the next century, elected councils came to share in running the patriarchate in the capital. In 1860 a written Armenian statute was drawn up to set the bounds of each council's work.

flags: Most of the window's evidence comes from Catholic-side writers (Chamich, Issaverdens, the Jesuits, Serpos) or from Ormanian (1912). The Gomidas account is Catholic-sourced and the prose says so; Ormanian does not name him but calls the patriarchate's measures 'weapons of war'.

The prose says only that the assembly asked Nadir to rule, which he did attend. Chamich's story that Nadir had Abraham gird on his sword is left out (Abraham's own text was not found to say it).

The corpus map's note that Abraham 'attended the accession ceremony of 20 February 1736' does not match his own chapter XLIII-XLIV; worth a fix in the staging file by the Library thread (not touched).
The 1722 date for the Afghan attack on Isfahan rests on Chamich's margin date 'A. D.1722,' at line 22236, just after the passage; the passage itself carries no year.

Avedik's sequel differs by source (Ormanian: Seven Towers 1703, abducted from Tenedos, taken to France 1710, condemned 1711; Issaverdens: seized on the way to Tenedos, held in Paris, released, died in peace; Chamich: went to Marseilles, died there as a Capuchin).
